name: Book of the Dead
info: The Book of the Dead is an ancient Egyptian funerary text of magic spells, written mostly on papyrus from the beginning of the New Kingdom to around 50 BC, meant to guide the dead through the underworld into the afterlife.

facts.made: Written by many priests over about 1,000 years, drawing on the older Pyramid Texts and Coffin Texts; each copy made to order by scribes and artists in funerary workshops
facts.form: A loose collection of some 192 known spells in hieroglyphic or hieratic script, in black and red ink on papyrus scrolls from about 1 m to 40 m long, often illustrated with vignettes
facts.where: Copies in many museums, among them the Papyrus of Ani and the Papyrus of Hunefer in the British Museum and the Book of the Dead of Kha in the Museo Egizio, Turin
facts.known: Spells of Coming Forth by Day; the Weighing of the Heart in Spell 125; the Negative Confession; Osiris, Anubis and Ammit the Devourer; the Field of Reeds; the Papyrus of Ani

t: There was no single Book of the Dead: each papyrus held its own selection of spells, and a fixed order appeared only with the Saite recension of the 25th and 26th Dynasties.
Its spells set out Egyptian beliefs about death: preserving the body, heart, name, ba and shadow, passing the guardians of the Duat and being judged before Osiris.
Named by Karl Richard Lepsius in 1842, it remains a vital source for Egyptian ideas of the afterlife and is studied today by the Book of the Dead Project in Bonn.
dyk: Many copies were prefabricated in workshops with spaces left for the owner's name; in the Papyrus of Ani the name "Ani" is in a different hand from the rest and is in places mis-spelt or left out.
ev: The Book of the Dead first develops in Thebes, its earliest spells known from the coffin of Queen Mentuhotep
From the beginning of the New Kingdom the spells are written mainly on papyrus scrolls
Spell 125, the Weighing of the Heart, is first known, from the reign of Hatshepsut and Thutmose III
The spells are ordered and numbered consistently in the Saite recension
The last use of the Book of the Dead
Karl Richard Lepsius publishes a translation, names it Todtenbuch and numbers its spells
The Papyrus of Ani is acquired by E. A. Wallis Budge and taken to the British Museum
Sections of the Book of the Dead are found on a 16-metre papyrus near the Step Pyramid of Djoser

sections.origins:
The Book of the Dead grew out of a tradition of funerary texts reaching back to the Old Kingdom. The first were the Pyramid Texts, carved on the walls of burial chambers from the pyramid of King Unas of the 5th Dynasty, around 2400 BC, and reserved for the pharaoh and later the queen. They aimed to help the dead king join the gods, above all his divine father Ra, in an afterlife then placed in the sky. By the end of the Old Kingdom regional governors and high officials had adopted them.

In the Middle Kingdom the Coffin Texts appeared, in a newer form of the language, with new spells and, for the first time, illustrations. Written mostly inside coffins, they were available to wealthy private people, a process described as the "democratization of the afterlife".

The Book of the Dead itself first developed in Thebes toward the beginning of the Second Intermediate Period, around 1700 BC. Its earliest known spells appear on the coffin of Queen Mentuhotep of the 16th Dynasty, among older Pyramid and Coffin Texts. Some new spells claimed an older origin: the rubric to Spell 30B says that Prince Hordjedef found it in the reign of King Menkaure, centuries before it is attested.
sections.content:
The Egyptian name, rw nw prt m hrw, is translated as Spells of Coming Forth by Day. Some 192 spells are known, though no manuscript contains them all. Some give the dead mystical knowledge or identify them with the gods; others preserve and reunite the parts of the person, protect the dead from hostile forces or guide them past the obstacles of the underworld. The texts were magical as well as religious: the Egyptians saw little distinction between the two, held that spoken and written words had creative power, and believed that knowing a thing's name gave power over it.

The spells describe the parts of a person to be kept: the body, the heart, the ka or life-force, the name, the ba that could "go forth by day" and the shadow, so that the dead might live on as an akh among the gods. The dead must pass gates and caverns guarded by armed creatures with names such as "He who dances in blood", pacified by the right spells. They might join Ra in his sun-barque or live in the Field of Reeds, where shabti figures did their labour.

In the Weighing of the Heart, shown in Spell 125, Anubis leads the dead before Osiris, they recite the Negative Confession, and their heart is weighed against Maat; a heart out of balance is eaten by Ammit, the Devourer.
sections.making:
A Book of the Dead was produced to order by scribes, for people preparing for their own funerals or for relatives of the newly dead. Copies were expensive: one source gives the price of a scroll as one deben of silver, perhaps half a labourer's annual pay. Many were prefabricated in funerary workshops, with spaces left for the owner's name.

Scrolls were made of joined sheets of papyrus, from as short as 1 m to 40 m long. New Kingdom copies were written in cursive hieroglyphs in columns separated by black lines, with illustrations framed above, below or between them; from the 21st Dynasty more copies are in hieratic, in horizontal lines. Most of the text was in carbon-based black ink, with red ochre ink for spell titles, instructions and the names of dangerous beings such as Apep. Vignettes ranged from lavish colour with gold leaf to simple line drawings. Several scribes and artists often worked on one copy, and some books have empty spaces where pictures were never added.

The text changed over time. Lavish vignettes marked the 19th Dynasty; cheaper hieratic scrolls appeared in the Third Intermediate Period; and in the 25th and 26th Dynasties the spells were revised and, for the first time, ordered and numbered consistently in what is called the Saite recension.
sections.reception:
The book was placed in the coffin or burial chamber of the dead. By the 17th Dynasty it was used not only by the royal family but by courtiers and officials, its spells then usually written on linen shrouds. Most later owners were also part of the elite: scribes, priests and officials. Early copies belonged roughly ten to men for every one to a woman, but in the Third Intermediate Period two were for women for every one for a man, and women owned about a third of the hieratic papyri of the Late and Ptolemaic periods.

Some owners seem to have chosen the spells they thought most vital. Certain spells continued to be inscribed separately on tomb walls and sarcophagi, and spells concerning the heart were inscribed on scarabs. In the Late and Ptolemaic periods copies followed the Saite recension, increasingly abbreviated, while new texts such as the Book of Breathing came into use. The last use was in the 1st century BC, though some of its motifs survived into Roman times.

Egyptologists differ on its moral teaching. John Taylor sees a pragmatic approach in Spells 30B and 125, which stop the heart from bearing witness against its owner; Ogden Goelet holds that a moral life was essential; Geraldine Pinch argues that success depended on knowing the judges' true names.
sections.survival:
The book's existence was known as early as the Middle Ages, long before it could be read, and because it came from tombs it was widely and wrongly thought to be an Egyptian equivalent of the Bible or Qur'an. Napoleon's invasion of Egypt in 1798 encouraged European interest; in 1805 Jean-Marcel Cadet made the first publication of a copy, and Champollion's decipherment of hieroglyphs followed in 1822.

In 1842 Karl Richard Lepsius published a translation of a Ptolemaic manuscript, coined the name Todtenbuch and introduced the spell numbering still in use. Édouard Naville produced a comparative edition between 1875 and 1886, and Samuel Birch of the British Museum published the first extensive English translation in 1867. The Papyrus of Ani, regarded as the finest surviving example, was found in Luxor in 1888 by Egyptians trading in illegal antiquities and acquired by E. A. Wallis Budge for the British Museum, where it remains.

Copies are held in many museums, among them the British Museum, the Museo Egizio in Turin, the Rijksmuseum van Oudheden in Leiden and the Royal Ontario Museum; the Joseph Smith Papyri survive only as fragments, many destroyed in modern times. In 2023 Egypt's Ministry of Antiquities announced sections on a 16-metre papyrus found near the Step Pyramid of Djoser, now called the Waziri Papyrus I.
sections.legacy:
The Book of the Dead is a vital source of information about Egyptian beliefs on death and the afterlife, and one of the few Egyptian religious texts with explicit moral content. For every "I have not" of the Negative Confession an unspoken "Thou shalt not" can be read, though it is less a revealed law, as the Ten Commandments are held to be, than a divine enforcement of everyday morality.

Budge's hieroglyphic editions and English translations of the Papyrus of Ani are still in wide circulation, though his translations are now considered inaccurate and out of date. Newer English translations were published by Raymond O. Faulkner in 1972 and Thomas George Allen in 1974, and further study has raised the count of known spells to 192. Paul Barguet's study of 1967 first showed common themes within the texts, which Egyptologists had thought had no internal structure.

In the 1970s Ursula Rößler-Köhler began a working group at the University of Bonn that became the Book of the Dead Project, which keeps documentation and photographs of 80% of the surviving copies and fragments and publishes monograph and manuscript series. Hieroglyphic fonts and digital printing have made publication cheaper, but much of the material in museums remains unpublished.

summary: The Book of the Dead, the Egyptian Spells of Coming Forth by Day, was a changing collection of some 192 funerary spells, developed from the Pyramid and Coffin Texts around 1700 BC and used until the 1st century BC. Its papyri, such as the Papyrus of Ani, are a main source for Egyptian beliefs about death, judgment and the afterlife.
